title: SMTP Service Extension for Secure SMTP over Transport Layer Security
summary: Describes the STARTTLS extension to SMTP, which lets a mail client and server upgrade a plain connection to one protected by TLS. This provides privacy and optional authentication against eavesdroppers. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3207 defines how an SMTP client and server can switch an existing connection to Transport Layer Security (TLS). This can protect their communication, but it does not protect every connection used to deliver a message.

questions: how to encrypt smtp with tls
subtitle: An SMTP extension that lets a client and server begin TLS on an existing connection.

tldr.problem: SMTP traffic can cross networks that neither endpoint trusts, exposing the conversation to monitoring or alteration.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises STARTTLS in its EHLO response. The client sends STARTTLS, the server replies 220, and both sides negotiate TLS before restarting SMTP.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3207 replaces RFC 2487 and is updated by RFC 7817. TLS protects one SMTP connection at a time, not an entire mail-delivery chain.

today: RFC 3207 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2487 and is updated by RFC 7817. The RFC defines TLS negotiation for an SMTP connection, not end-to-end protection for a message.

sections.title: Why SMTP Uses TLS
sections.content:
SMTP clients and servers normally communicate without encryption. Traffic may pass through routers that neither endpoint controls, allowing a third party to monitor or alter the conversation.

RFC 3207 defines an SMTP extension for negotiating TLS on that connection. TLS can provide privacy and authentication between the two SMTP agents. The RFC obsoletes RFC 2487.
sections.plainLanguage: SMTP traffic may cross networks that the client and server do not control. TLS can protect the connection between those two agents from reading or alteration.

sections.title: Advertising the STARTTLS Extension
sections.content:
The extension adds the STARTTLS keyword to the server's response to EHLO, and defines a STARTTLS command with no parameters. Advertising the keyword tells the client that the server can currently negotiate TLS.

The extension adds no parameters to other SMTP commands. A client decides whether to request TLS based on its policy and the server's advertised capability.
sections.plainLanguage: The server advertises whether it can negotiate TLS by listing STARTTLS after EHLO. The client can then request the change with a command that has no parameters.

sections.title: Starting TLS on the Connection
sections.content:
After receiving STARTTLS, the server can reply 220 to proceed, 501 for a syntax error, or 454 when TLS is temporarily unavailable. After a 220 reply, the client must begin the TLS handshake before sending another SMTP command.

If the client receives 454, local policy determines whether it continues without TLS, retries later, or gives up. A publicly referenced SMTP server must not require STARTTLS for local mail delivery, so the extension does not break delivery to servers that do not support it.
sections.plainLanguage: A 220 reply means the client must start the TLS handshake before continuing SMTP. A 454 reply leaves the client to decide whether to retry, continue without TLS, or stop.

sections.title: Restarting SMTP After the Handshake
sections.content:
After TLS negotiation, both endpoints assess the privacy and authentication achieved. If either side is not satisfied, the client should send QUIT, or the server should refuse further commands with 554.

The SMTP session resets after the handshake. Both sides discard information learned before TLS, and the client should send a new EHLO. The server must not advertise STARTTLS again after TLS is active.

The extension can also be used on the Submission port. RFC 3207 says it may be especially useful there because that service is not a publicly referenced SMTP server.
sections.plainLanguage: After TLS starts, the client and server check whether the connection meets their security needs. They discard pre-TLS session information and begin SMTP again with a fresh EHLO exchange.

sections.title: Limits of Connection Security
sections.content:
STARTTLS protects one SMTP connection, not the full route from the message author to the recipient. A message can pass through more than two SMTP servers, and authenticating an SMTP client does not authenticate the message's author.

An active attacker may remove the server's STARTTLS offer or alter the negotiation. Clients and servers must be configurable to require successful TLS for selected hosts. Both endpoints must check the handshake result and discard pre-handshake information.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects only the SMTP connection where it is negotiated, so another delivery step may still be unprotected. A client or server can require TLS to avoid continuing in clear text.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 2487
sections.content:
RFC 3207 revises RFC 2487. Its listed changes include more discussion of man-in-the-middle attacks, clearer guidance about when servers advertise STARTTLS, and changed client requirements after a 220 response.

The revision also clarifies certificate verification, adds discussion of the Submission port, and corrects the example so the client sends a new EHLO after TLS negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: This revision clarifies how clients and servers handle TLS negotiation and improves the security discussion. It also fixes the example to show a new EHLO after the handshake.
